records.source: וַיֵּ֥רַע אֶל־יוֹנָ֖ה רָעָ֣ה גְדוֹלָ֑ה וַיִּ֖חַר לֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And it was evil to Jonah, an evil great, and it burned to him.
pieces: But to Jonah this seemed a great wrong, and he became angry.

L.1: But it was evil to Jonah, a great evil, and he became hot [with anger].

R.1: But Jonah was very upset about this, and he became angry.

decisions.choice: it was evil to Jonah, a great evil: Jonah was deeply displeased
decisions.reason: The book's word for evil and disaster (see 1:2) comes back with the word "great". Nineveh turned from evil and God turned from disaster; now Jonah thinks it evil, a great one, that God has done so. The verse turns the words of the story against him.

decisions.choice: it burned to him: he became angry
decisions.reason: In Hebrew, anger "burns". The same verb comes in the LORD's question, "Is it good that it burns to you?" (4:4, 9).

decisions.choice: a great evil (L); a great wrong (B); very upset (R); hot [with anger] (L); angry (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "evil" and "great", so the reader can see both words return. Balanced says "a great wrong"; Readable says how Jonah felt.

records.heading: Jonah's anger

records.source: וַיִּתְפַּלֵּ֨ל אֶל־יְהוָ֜ה וַיֹּאמַ֗ר אָנָּ֤ה יְהוָה֙ הֲלוֹא־זֶ֣ה דְבָרִ֗י עַד־הֱיוֹתִי֙ עַל־אַדְמָתִ֔י עַל־כֵּ֥ן קִדַּ֖מְתִּי לִבְרֹ֣חַ תַּרְשִׁ֑ישָׁה כִּ֣י יָדַ֗עְתִּי כִּ֤י אַתָּה֙ אֵֽל־חַנּ֣וּן וְרַח֔וּם אֶ֤רֶךְ אַפַּ֨יִם֙ וְרַב־חֶ֔סֶד וְנִחָ֖ם עַל־הָרָעָֽה׃
records.gloss: And he prayed to Yahweh and said, Please, Yahweh, [was] not this my word while I was on my land? Therefore I acted first to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you [are] a God gracious and compassionate, long of anger and great of loyal love, and relenting concerning the evil.
pieces: He prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "Please, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, did I not say this while I was still in my own country? That is why I hurried to run away to Tarshish. For I knew that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are a God of grace and tender compassion, slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love, and one who relents from sending disaster.

L.2: And he prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, "Please, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, [was] this not my word while I was still in my own land? That is why I acted first to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} [are] a God gracious and compassionate, long of anger, and great in steadfast love, and relenting concerning the evil.

R.2: Jonah prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "Please, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, I said this would happen when I was still at home! That is why I hurried to run away to Tarshish. I knew that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are a God of kindness and tender mercy. You are slow to become angry. Your faithful love is great. You change {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} mind about punishing people.

decisions.choice: a God gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, great in loyal love: the words of Exodus 34:6
decisions.reason: When the LORD passed before Moses he proclaimed himself "a God compassionate and gracious, long of anger, and great in steadfast love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). Jonah quotes it with the first two words in the other order, as Joel 2:13 and Psalm 145:8 have them, leaves out "and faithfulness", and adds "relenting concerning the evil", as Joel 2:13 does. Israel praised God in these words (Psalm 86:15; 103:8; Nehemiah 9:17); Jonah uses them as a complaint.

decisions.choice: relenting concerning the evil: turning back from the disaster he has threatened
decisions.reason: This is the verb of 3:9-10, used with the book's word for evil and disaster (see 1:2). Jonah has seen God do exactly this for Nineveh.

decisions.choice: was this not my word? Jonah gives the reason he fled
decisions.reason: Only now does the reader learn why Jonah ran away in chapter 1: not from fear, but because he knew God would forgive Nineveh, and he did not want that. The book does not say what lay behind it. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, Israel's great enemy, and Jonah's anger may be that of a man who wanted justice on the city instead of mercy.

decisions.choice: I acted first: I tried to forestall it
decisions.reason: The verb means to go before, to act ahead of time. Jonah ran to Tarshish to get ahead of what he knew God would do, so as not to be the one who brought Nineveh its warning.

decisions.choice: the words of Exodus 34:6 at each level, with "gracious" and "compassionate" in Jonah's order; steadfast love (L); faithful love (B, R)
decisions.reason: Each level reuses its wording of Exodus 34:6, as set for Jonah 4:2: "long of anger" and "great in steadfast love" at Literal, "slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love" at Balanced, "slow to become angry" and "faithful love is great" at Readable. For that reason *hesed* here is "steadfast love" at Literal, as in Exodus, not "loyal love" as elsewhere in the prophets. Readable addresses God as "you" throughout and says "change your mind about punishing people" for relenting from disaster.

decisions.choice: Please, LORD (all levels); I said this would happen (R)
decisions.reason: "Please, LORD" is the same cry the sailors used (1:14), and every level keeps it. Readable turns the question "was this not my word?" into the statement it implies. Jonah's prayer is in prose, as the chapter is, and his words run to the end of verse 3.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֣ה יְהוָ֔ה קַח־נָ֥א אֶת־נַפְשִׁ֖י מִמֶּ֑נִּי כִּ֛י ט֥וֹב מוֹתִ֖י מֵחַיָּֽי׃ס
records.gloss: And now, Yahweh, take, please, my life from me, for better [is] my death than my life.
pieces: So now, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, please take my life from me, for death is better for me than life."

L.3: And now, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, take my life from me, please, for my death [is] better than my life."

R.3: So now, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, please let me die. I would rather be dead than alive."

decisions.choice: take my life: Elijah's prayer in 1 Kings 19:4
decisions.reason: Elijah, fleeing from Jezebel, sat under a broom tree and said, "Now, LORD, take my life, for I am not better than my fathers" (1 Kings 19:4). Jonah prays the same words, but Elijah was in despair because his work seemed to fail; Jonah is angry because his work has succeeded. 4:8 echoes the same verse again.

decisions.choice: take my life (L, B); let me die (R); death is better for me than life (B); rather be dead than alive (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "take my life", as in 1 Kings 19:4, with "LORD" and no "O", as set for the prophets. Balanced and Readable turn "my death is better than my life" into everyday words, the same in 4:8. The double quotation mark closes Jonah's prayer.

records.gloss: And said Yahweh, Is it doing good [that] it burns to you?
pieces: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "Are you right to be angry?"

L.4: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "Is it good that you are burning [with anger]?"

R.4: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "Do you have a right to be angry?"

decisions.choice: is it good? Are you right to be angry?
decisions.reason: The word means "doing well", and so either "is it right" or, used as an adverb, "very" ("are you so very angry?"). Most read it as the question whether Jonah's anger is justified. It is a question, not a statement, and Jonah does not answer it until verse 9.

decisions.choice: Is it good that you are burning [with anger]? (L); Are you right to be angry? (B); Do you have a right to be angry? (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the picture of burning anger (see 4:1). Balanced and Readable give the question in everyday words, and use the same words in verse 9.

records.heading: The plant and the great city

records.source: וַיֵּצֵ֤א יוֹנָה֙ מִן־הָעִ֔יר וַיֵּ֖שֶׁב מִקֶּ֣דֶם לָעִ֑יר וַיַּעַשׂ֩ ל֨וֹ שָׁ֜ם סֻכָּ֗ה וַיֵּ֤שֶׁב תַּחְתֶּ֨יהָ֙ בַּצֵּ֔ל עַ֚ד אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִרְאֶ֔ה מַה־יִּהְיֶ֖ה בָּעִֽיר׃
records.gloss: And went out Jonah from the city and sat east of the city; and he made for himself there a booth and sat under it in the shade, until he would see what would be in the city.
pieces: Jonah went out of the city and sat down to the east of it. He made himself a shelter there and sat under it in the shade, waiting to see what would become of the city.

L.5: And Jonah went out from the city and sat east of the city. And he made for himself a booth there and sat under it in the shade, until he could see what would happen in the city.

R.5: Jonah went out of the city and sat down at a place east of it. There he made a shelter for himself and sat in its shade. He waited to see what would happen to the city.

decisions.choice: Jonah went out: what Jonah did after the LORD's question, or what he had done earlier
alternatives: Jonah had gone out, before God relented (3:10)
decisions.reason: The verse may continue the story: after the LORD's question Jonah went out to watch, still hoping that the city would be destroyed. Or it may step back to the time before 3:10, when the forty days were still running. The verb form allows both. Either way, Jonah sits and waits to see whether Nineveh will fall.

decisions.choice: a booth: a rough shelter of branches
decisions.reason: The word is used of the temporary huts of the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:42) and of shelters in a field (Isaiah 1:8). It gave some shade, but not enough, as the next verse shows.

decisions.choice: booth (L); shelter (B, R); what would happen in (L); what would become of (B); what would happen to (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "shelter" because the reader may not know what a booth is (m2).

records.source: וַיְמַ֣ן יְהוָֽה־אֱ֠לֹהִים קִיקָי֞וֹן וַיַּ֣עַל׀מֵעַ֣ל לְיוֹנָ֗ה לִֽהְי֥וֹת צֵל֙ עַל־רֹאשׁ֔וֹ לְהַצִּ֥יל ל֖וֹ מֵרָֽעָת֑וֹ וַיִּשְׂמַ֥ח יוֹנָ֛ה עַל־הַקִּֽיקָי֖וֹן שִׂמְחָ֥ה גְדוֹלָֽה׃
records.gloss: And appointed Yahweh God a qiqayon, and it went up over Jonah to be shade over his head, to deliver him from his evil; and rejoiced Jonah over the qiqayon [with] a joy great.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} God appointed a leafy plant, and it grew up over Jonah to give shade over his head and to save him from his misery. Jonah was overjoyed about the plant.

L.6: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God appointed a plant, and it went up over Jonah to be shade over his head, to deliver him from his misery; and Jonah rejoiced over the plant [with] a great joy.

R.6: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God sent a leafy plant, and it grew up over Jonah. It gave shade to his head and eased his misery. Jonah was very happy about the plant.

decisions.choice: a plant: a fast-growing, broad-leaved plant whose kind is not known for certain
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word is used only in this chapter. It is often taken to be the castor-oil plant, which grows quickly and has large leaves; the Greek translation calls it a gourd. Early Christian readers debated the word: Jerome's Latin rendered it "ivy", and Augustine recorded the stir that this caused when the new rendering was read in church. The story needs only a plant that grew fast and gave shade. These descriptions of the ancient translations are written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: to deliver him from his misery: "misery" is again the book's word for evil
alternatives: to shade him from his misery
decisions.reason: The book's word for evil and disaster (see 1:2) is used here for Jonah's discomfort, and perhaps also his bad temper (4:1). The verb "deliver" sounds like the word for "shade" just before it, a play the verse makes on purpose.

decisions.choice: the LORD God: the two names together, only here in Jonah
decisions.reason: The book calls God "the LORD" and "God". Here, as God moves from Nineveh to deal with his prophet, both names stand together, as in the garden story of Genesis 2-3. The next two appointments, the worm and the wind, are by "God".

decisions.choice: Jonah rejoiced with a great joy: the only time he is glad in the book
decisions.reason: "Great" comes again (see 1:2). Jonah's great anger (4:1) becomes great joy, over a plant.

decisions.choice: appointed (L, B); sent (R); a plant (L); a leafy plant (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Appointed" keeps the same word for each thing God appoints (2:1); Readable says "sent". Balanced and Readable say "leafy" because the plant gave shade, without naming a kind (m1). Balanced says "overjoyed" for "rejoiced with a great joy".

records.source: וַיְמַ֤ן הָֽאֱלֹהִים֙ תּוֹלַ֔עַת בַּעֲל֥וֹת הַשַּׁ֖חַר לַֽמָּחֳרָ֑ת וַתַּ֥ךְ אֶת־הַקִּֽיקָי֖וֹן וַיִּיבָֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And appointed the God a worm at the going up of the dawn on the next day, and it struck the qiqayon, and it withered.
pieces: But at dawn the next day God appointed a worm, which attacked the plant so that it withered.

L.7: And God appointed a worm when the dawn came up on the next day, and it struck the plant, and it withered.

R.7: But early the next morning God sent a worm. It chewed the plant, and the plant dried up.

decisions.choice: a worm struck the plant: a small creature brings down what God gave
decisions.reason: God appoints a worm as he appointed the fish and the plant. The verb "struck" is used of the sun striking Jonah in the next verse. A grub or worm boring into the stem would kill a plant quickly.

decisions.choice: appointed (L, B); sent (R); struck (L); attacked (B); chewed (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 6, Literal and Balanced say "appointed", Readable "sent". Readable says what a worm does to a plant.

records.source: וַיְהִ֣י׀כִּזְרֹ֣חַ הַשֶּׁ֗מֶשׁ וַיְמַ֨ן אֱלֹהִ֜ים ר֤וּחַ קָדִים֙ חֲרִישִׁ֔ית וַתַּ֥ךְ הַשֶּׁ֛מֶשׁ עַל־רֹ֥אשׁ יוֹנָ֖ה וַיִּתְעַלָּ֑ף וַיִּשְׁאַ֤ל אֶת־נַפְשׁוֹ֙ לָמ֔וּת וַיֹּ֕אמֶר ט֥וֹב מוֹתִ֖י מֵחַיָּֽי׃
records.gloss: And it happened, as rose the sun, and appointed God a wind east scorching, and struck the sun on [the] head of Jonah, and he grew faint; and he asked his life to die, and said, Better [is] my death than my life.
pieces: When the sun came up, God appointed a scorching wind from the east, and the sun beat down on Jonah's head until he grew faint. He prayed that he might die, and he said, "Death is better for me than life."

L.8: And it happened, when the sun rose, that God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun struck the head of Jonah, and he grew faint; and he asked for himself that he might die, and said, "My death [is] better than my life."

R.8: When the sun came up, God sent a hot wind from the east. The sun beat down on Jonah's head, and he became weak and faint. He asked to die. "I would rather be dead than alive," he said.

decisions.choice: a scorching east wind: the hot wind off the desert
decisions.reason: The east wind blows in from the desert, hot and dry, and withers plants (Genesis 41:6; Ezekiel 17:10; Hosea 13:15). The word for "scorching" is used only here and its sense is not certain; it may mean hot, sultry or still.

decisions.choice: he asked for himself that he might die: the words of 1 Kings 19:4
decisions.reason: The phrase is the same as Elijah's under the broom tree, as Jonah's prayer in verse 3 was. Jonah repeats his own words from verse 3, "my death is better than my life".

decisions.choice: appointed (L, B); sent (R); he asked for himself that he might die (L); he prayed that he might die (B); He asked to die (R)
decisions.reason: Each level reuses its wording of 1 Kings 19:4 for the request to die (m2) and its own wording of verse 3 for Jonah's words.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶל־יוֹנָ֔ה הַהֵיטֵ֥ב חָרָֽה־לְךָ֖ עַל־הַקִּֽיקָי֑וֹן וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הֵיטֵ֥ב חָֽרָה־לִ֖י עַד־מָֽוֶת׃
records.gloss: And said God to Jonah, Is it doing good [that] it burns to you over the qiqayon? And he said, Doing good [that] it burns to me, to death.
pieces: But God said to Jonah, "Are you right to be angry about the plant?" "I am right to be angry," he said, "angry enough to die!"

L.9: And God said to Jonah, "Is it good that you are burning [with anger] about the plant?" And he said, "It is good that I am burning [with anger], even to death."

R.9: But God said to Jonah, "Do you have a right to be angry about the plant?" "Yes, I do," Jonah answered. "I am so angry I could die!"

decisions.choice: Jonah answers the question of verse 4 with God's own words
decisions.reason: God asks again, now about the plant, and Jonah throws the words back: "it is good" that he is angry. "To death" means as angry as a person can be, angry enough to wish to die (Judges 16:16; Matthew 26:38).

decisions.choice: the same wording as verse 4 for the question, at each level
decisions.reason: Each level keeps its wording of verse 4, so that the reader can hear the question repeated. Readable makes Jonah's answer a plain "Yes".

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֔ה אַתָּ֥ה חַ֨סְתָּ֙ עַל־הַקִּ֣יקָי֔וֹן אֲשֶׁ֛ר לֹא־עָמַ֥לְתָּ בּ֖וֹ וְלֹ֣א גִדַּלְתּ֑וֹ שֶׁבִּן־לַ֥יְלָה הָיָ֖ה וּבִן־לַ֥יְלָה אָבָֽד׃
records.gloss: And said Yahweh, You, you had pity on the qiqayon, for which you did not toil and you did not make it grow, which as a son of a night came to be and as a son of a night perished.
pieces: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "You took pity on the plant, though you did not work for it or make it grow. It sprang up in a night and died in a night.

L.10: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "You had pity on the plant, for which you did not labor, and which you did not make grow, which came to be [as] the son of a night and perished [as] the son of a night.

R.10: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "You cared about this plant, though you did nothing to make it grow. It grew up in one night and died just as quickly.

decisions.choice: you had pity: you felt for it, you would have spared it
decisions.reason: The verb means to look with pity on something and to spare it (Ezekiel 20:17; Joel 2:17). The same verb is God's in verse 11. The argument moves from the lesser to the greater: if Jonah grieves over a plant, how much more should God care for a city.

decisions.choice: the son of a night: what grew up in one night
decisions.reason: In Hebrew, "son of" can describe something by what belongs to it: "a son of a night" is something that lasts a night. The plant came up in a night and was gone in a night.

decisions.choice: had pity (L); took pity (B); cared about (R); [as] the son of a night (L); in a night (B, R)
decisions.reason: Each level uses the same verb here and in verse 11 (m1). Literal keeps the idiom "the son of a night"; Balanced and Readable say what it means (m2). Readable joins "you did not labor" and "you did not make it grow" into one phrase.

records.source: וַֽאֲנִי֙ לֹ֣א אָח֔וּס עַל־נִינְוֵ֖ה הָעִ֣יר הַגְּדוֹלָ֑ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר יֶשׁ־בָּ֡הּ הַרְבֵּה֩ מִֽשְׁתֵּים־עֶשְׂרֵ֨ה רִבּ֜וֹ אָדָ֗ם אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־יָדַע֙ בֵּין־יְמִינ֣וֹ לִשְׂמֹאל֔וֹ וּבְהֵמָ֖ה רַבָּֽה׃
records.gloss: And I, shall I not have pity on Nineveh, the great city, in which there are more than twelve myriads of humans who do not know between their right hand and their left, and animals many?
pieces: And should I not take pity on Nineveh, that great city, with more than 120,000 people in it who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many animals as well?"

L.11: And I, should I not have pity on Nineveh, the great city, in which there are more than 120,000 human beings who do not know between their right hand and their left, and many animals?"

R.11: So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh? More than 120,000 people live there who cannot tell their right hand from their left. And there are many animals too."

decisions.choice: who do not know their right hand from their left: who are helpless, without understanding
alternatives: people without the knowledge of God's law
decisions.reason: The phrase may describe the whole population as morally helpless, lacking the understanding God gives, or it may count the city's small children, too young to tell right from left. The text does not explain it. Either way, they are people in need of mercy, not judgment.

decisions.choice: more than 120,000: twelve times ten thousand
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "more than twelve ten-thousands". The number shows how many lives were at stake, whether it counts all the city's people or only its children (m1).

decisions.choice: should I not have pity? The book ends with God's question
decisions.reason: The LORD asks Jonah, and the reader, whether he should not care for a great city full of people, and even its animals. The book does not give Jonah's answer. It closes on God's compassion for a foreign and enemy city, the very thing Jonah confessed in 4:2.

decisions.choice: have pity (L); take pity (B); care about (R); human beings (L); people (B, R); 120,000 (all levels)
decisions.reason: The verb is the same as in verse 10 at each level. The number is written in figures, as numbers over ninety-nine are. Readable states the facts about the city in sentences of their own after the question. The double quotation mark closes the LORD's words and the book.
